title: Paint the target after you shoot

probes.question: In the Texas sharpshooter fallacy, when is the target drawn?
True or false: the fallacy means inferring meaning from what is essentially a random distribution of data points.

image.alt: A yellow wooden board on posts with many small bullet holes scattered around a dark square.

panels.text: A man in Texas fires a gun at the side of a barn. The bullets land in a scatter.
Then he paints a target around the tightest cluster of holes and calls himself a sharpshooter.
Statisticians call this the Texas sharpshooter fallacy: finding meaning in what is really a random scatter of data points. It is the rhetorical cousin of data dredging, or p-hacking.
The mathematician John Venn used the target-chalking analogy in 1866, though similar stories are older. Ask for the pattern to be named before you look at the data.
